about: Spoken-register guidance for voice agents, per call language and business type. AI-drafted 10 Oct 2026 and expanded 11 Oct 2026 (founder decisions 3, 10 Oct, and the 11 Oct spoken-style rules). EVERY entry here is needs_native_review except prompt_examples (founder approved 14 Oct 2026, see its note): the founder reviews them on the admin screen Ops > Spoken style, whose published edits are stored in the database and layered over this file (calevate_shared.spoken_style.install_published). What each part is for: register is the one-line description of how the language is spoken; word_swaps pairs a formal or written form (left) with what people actually say (right), and the ones named in prompt_swaps go into every agent's prompt in that language, while the whole list guides the script writer, the test callers and the test checks; fillers are the spoken tags and light fillers people use; number_rules and punctuation say how numbers and sentences are written for a voice; examples are example exchanges per business type that show HOW to speak, never facts (no price, time, address or stock level, so an agent cannot repeat a made-up fact); openings are a starter's greeting; spelled_address is how an agent whose caller follows along on a screen spells a web address (D-906): each letter by its English name in the language's letters, a comma between, so a spelled letter is not heard as a word of the language. SCRIPT (founder, 23 Oct 2026, D-861, reversing the 11 Oct English-letters rule): every spoken line is written wholly in the language's own letters, English words and amounts too (కాల్, డెలివరీ, వన్ ట్వంటీ రూపీస్; कॉल, डिलीवरी), after the founder heard a competitor's agent written that way as very human-sounding on Cartesia; every line rewritten to that rule is needs_native_review. Register sources for te-IN: Telugu has a literary register (grandhika) and a spoken standard (vyavaharika, the sishta vyavaharika of educated everyday speech), the latter championed by Gidugu Venkata Ramamurthy (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gidugu_Venkata_Ramamurthy; https://www.deccanchronicle.com/lifestyle/culture-and-society/telugu-language-day-commemorates-gidugu-revolutionary-behind-simple-telugu-usage-1983163). Telugu-English code-mixing ('Tenglish') is extensively used in Hyderabad (Dutta and Rajeswari, Texas Linguistics Forum 2015, https://asol.ling.utexas.edu/salsa/proceedings/2015/Dutta.pdf); Standard and Telangana Telugu differences and code-mixing in speech are studied in Sravani, Kameswari and Mamidi 2021 (https://aclanthology.org/2021.calcs-1.1). Voice facts (Cartesia, read 11 Oct 2026): sonic-3.6 lists Telugu (te); it varies pacing and intonation to the transcript without SSML, pause length adapts to the sentence, and disfluencies such as 'uhm' give a thinking pace (https://docs.cartesia.ai/build-with-cartesia/tts-models/latest); full, punctuated sentences ending in . ? or ! give the best pacing (https://docs.cartesia.ai/build-with-cartesia/sonic-3-5/prompting-tips). Code-switching is documented only for Hindi written in Latin script; Telugu-English mixing is UNVERIFIED in the vendor docs and confirmed only by the founder's ear test ("whole chilli", "call", "kg" spoken naturally). The number style (prices, quantities and times in English words as shop people say them) is the founder's decision of 11 Oct 2026; Cartesia's own guidance would let the model normalise digits, which the founder's ear test overrode for Telugu calls.

te-IN.register: Everyday spoken Telugu (vyavaharika, never grandhika), neutral for Telangana and Andhra, every word in Telugu letters, English words too (ఆర్డర్, కాల్). అండి and గారు by situation, not in every sentence.

fillers.use: Acknowledging what the caller said or asked for.
Short yes, or showing you are listening.
Mild surprise or 'is that so?' after news from the caller.
A tag asking for agreement: '..., కదా?'
A casual 'what?', as in 'ఏంటి ప్రాబ్లం?'
Before checking something or looking it up.
'I mean' or 'that is', before rephrasing.
Okay, between steps.
A polite yes.
'Sure, will do' to a request.
'Go ahead, tell me' when the caller starts.
'Good' when the caller agrees to a next step.
Sympathy when the caller has a problem: 'అయ్యో, సారీ అండి.'
Reassuring after the caller apologises or declines.

number_rules.text: Prices the English way, as shop people say them, written in Telugu letters: 120 rupees is "వన్ ట్వంటీ రూపీస్", 250 is "టూ ఫిఫ్టీ రూపీస్", 1,500 is "ఫిఫ్టీన్ హండ్రెడ్ రూపీస్". Never the rupee sign or digits.
Big amounts as people say them, in Telugu letters: "సెవెంటీ లాక్స్", "వన్ పాయింట్ ఫైవ్ క్రోర్స్".
Quantities and units the English way, in Telugu letters: "వన్ కేజీ", "హాఫ్ కేజీ", "టూ లీటర్స్", "టూ బీహెచ్కే", "ట్వెల్వ్ హండ్రెడ్ స్క్వేర్ ఫీట్".
A time the caller said goes back in the same words: they said "సిక్స్", say "సిక్స్". A time you bring up, as people say them: "పొద్దున పది గంటలకు", "మధ్యాహ్నం రెండు గంటలకు", "సాయంత్రం ఐదున్నరకు".
రేపు, ఎల్లుండి and ఈరోజు as they are; weekdays in Telugu letters as people say them: "మండే", "సాటర్డే".

Phone numbers, OTPs and codes one digit at a time, the English way in Telugu letters: "నైన్ ఎయిట్ ఫోర్ నైన్". A mobile has ten digits: given four, ask for the other six ("ఇంకా సిక్స్ డిజిట్స్ చెప్తారా?"), never read the four back.
Small everyday counts stay Telugu (రెండు నిమిషాలు, ఒక్క సెకండ్); a price or a quantity is said the English way, in Telugu letters.

punctuation.text: Short sentences, one idea each. Split a long sentence into two.
A comma where you would take a breath: "సరే అండి, ఒక్క నిమిషం."
A question mark on every question and a full stop at the end of every other sentence.
No dashes, slashes, brackets, ellipses, quotation marks, bullets or emoji: the voice reads them or stumbles on them.
No dotted abbreviations: "Dr Ravi", never "Dr. Ravi"; say "rupees", never "Rs".
Every word in Telugu letters, English words too: డెలివరీ, not delivery.
Two choices as two short questions, "హోల్ చిల్లీ కావాలా, పౌడర్ కావాలా?", rather than a list joined with లేదా.

prompt_examples.note: In-call examples for the SPOKEN REGISTER section (D-778, D-861): one idea per sentence, a question mark on every question (often two choices), and the caller's own words said back. D-894: a reaction only where it fits, so the first answer asks straight on with no opener, and a time the caller said in English words goes back in those words. Wording founder 27 Oct 2026 (the first and third replaced, the second kept), replacing the 23 Oct set whose every turn opened with a reaction. Every word in the language's own letters; NEEDS NATIVE-SPEAKER REVIEW. Introduced as how a turn sounds, never words to copy, and carrying no fact. Edited here, not on Ops > Spoken style.
exchanges: అలాగే అండి, రేపు. పొద్దున వీలవుతుందా, సాయంత్రమా?
సాటర్డే ఈవెనింగ్ సిక్స్ కి అండి. మీ పేరు చెప్తారా?

candidate_prompt_examples.note: More in-call examples carrying the spoken words the agent tests miss (thanks, help, sorry, details, quantity), drafted for D-829. language_pack.note: D-830 language pack: the one platform block for how an agent speaks Telugu, full when Telugu is the primary language, compact (the first say_english, avoid and exchanges) when it is an extra. AI-drafted, measured by scripts/register_eval (--variants pack-en,pack-native,...); no prompt reads it until review is founder_approved and ship names the form the eval chose, e.g. {"form": "native", "avoid": "none"}. avoid lists the list words the 19 Oct 2026 production eval saw most, most frequent first.
language_pack.talk_en: Everyday spoken Telugu as people talk on the phone, neutral for Telangana and Andhra, in Telugu script, never bookish or newsreader Telugu. అండి and గారు by situation, not in every sentence.

talk: మనం ఫోన్ లో మామూలుగా ఎలా మాట్లాడతామో అలాగే మాట్లాడండి, రోజూ మాట్లాడే సింపుల్ తెలుగు లో.
తెలంగాణ వాళ్ళకీ ఆంధ్ర వాళ్ళకీ ఒకేలా అర్థమయ్యేలా చెప్పండి.
తెలుగు మాటలూ, ఇంగ్లీష్ మాటలూ, అన్నీ తెలుగు అక్షరాల్లోనే రాయండి.
అండి, గారు అప్పుడప్పుడు వాడండి, ప్రతి సెంటెన్స్ లో కాదు.

fillers.use: Acknowledging what the caller said or asked for.
A polite yes, or showing you are listening.
'I see' after news from the caller.
Before checking something or looking it up.
'I mean', before rephrasing.
'Of course' to a request.
'Go ahead, tell me' when the caller starts.
Reassuring after the caller apologises or declines.

number_rules.text: Prices and quantities in words, the way shop people say them on the phone, in Hindi or English words, written in Devanagari: "एक सौ बीस रुपये" or "वन ट्वेंटी", "एक किलो". Never the rupee sign or digits.
A time the caller said, back in their words: they said "सिक्स", say "सिक्स", never "छह बजे". A time you bring up, as people say them: "शाम पाँच बजे", "साढ़े दस".
Phone numbers, OTPs and codes one digit at a time.

punctuation.text: Short sentences, one idea each, a comma where you would take a breath.
A question mark on every question; end other sentences with । or a full stop.
No dashes, slashes, brackets, ellipses, quotation marks, bullets or emoji.
Every word in Devanagari, English words too: डिलीवरी, not delivery.

prompt_examples.note: In-call examples for the SPOKEN REGISTER section (D-778), rewritten 23 Oct 2026 for D-861 to teach punctuation that breathes: a comma after an opener, one idea per sentence, a question mark on every question (often two choices), an occasional exclamation for warmth, and the caller's answer said back before the next question. Written by us, every word in the language's own letters. The founder approved the approach and asked for them on calls (23 Oct 2026); the wording NEEDS NATIVE-SPEAKER REVIEW. Introduced as how a turn sounds, never words to copy, and carrying no fact. Edited here, not on Ops > Spoken style.

en-IN.register: Simple, warm Indian English as people speak on the phone. Sir or madam once, not every line. Mix in Hindi or Telugu words if the caller does.

_default: Hi, do you have this in stock?
Yes, we have it. How much would you need?
I'll tell you later, I'm a bit busy now.
No problem at all. Call us whenever it suits you.
retail: Do you have dry red chilli?
Yes, we do. How much do you need?
I don't have the delivery details with me. Which area are you in?
clinic: I want to see the doctor. Can I get an appointment?
Sure. What would you like to see the doctor for?
I've had a fever for two days.
Understood. Which day and time suits you?
real_estate: Do you have 2 BHK flats in the project?
Yes, we do. What budget are you looking at?
I'd like to see the site first.
Of course. Which day can you come for a site visit?
insurance: When is my policy due for renewal?
I don't have your policy details with me. Which policy is it?
Okay. Tell me your name and policy number and I'll note it down.
education: Are admissions open for the spoken English course?
Yes, they are. Which class is the student in?
Okay. Would you like to attend a demo class first?
local_services: Is there a slot for a haircut tomorrow?
Okay. May I have your name?
automobile: I need my bike serviced. When can I bring it?
Okay. Which day can you bring it in?
